summary: Specifies algorithms for encoding or hashing an arbitrary string to a point on an elliptic curve. This is a building block for many cryptographic protocols. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC specifies ways to turn any byte string into an elliptic-curve point. It explains how to choose an encoding and avoid bias, timing leaks, and confusion between different uses.

questions: how to map a string to a curve point
encode to curve vs hash to curve
what is the difference between encode to curve and hash to curve
why does hashing to curves need domain separation
subtitle: Algorithms for mapping arbitrary byte strings to elliptic-curve points.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic protocols need a secure way to map arbitrary inputs to elliptic-curve points. A poorly chosen method can create biased outputs or leak information through timing.
tldr.mechanism: The algorithms expand and hash input into field elements, map those elements deterministically to curve points, and clear the cofactor to reach the prime-order subgroup.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines uniform and nonuniform encodings, recommended suites for named curves, and guidance for implementations and new suites. It is an Informational CFRG document.

facts.label: Core functions
facts.value: Hash to field, map to curve, clear cofactor

today: RFC 9380 is an Informational RFC that represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group. It is not an Internet Standards Track specification.

sections.title: Why Hash Inputs to Curves
sections.content:
Some cryptographic protocols need to turn an arbitrary byte string, such as a password or protocol message, into a point on an elliptic curve. RFC 9380 gives algorithms for several curve families and explains how to define a suite for another curve.

A mapping takes a field element to a curve point. An encoding first turns an arbitrary byte string into field elements and then applies a mapping. The RFC does not cover converting points to or from serialized byte strings.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol may need a curve point that depends on an arbitrary input string. This document defines how to calculate that point in a consistent way.

sections.title: The Main Construction
sections.content:
The construction uses three functions. hash_to_field produces one or more field elements from the message and a domain separation tag. map_to_curve converts each field element to a point, and clear_cofactor moves the result into the curve's prime-order subgroup.

Hashing to a field must avoid rejection sampling, which is difficult to implement in constant time. The RFC's expansion methods produce enough bytes to limit bias when converting them to field elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The process has three stages: derive field elements from the input, calculate curve points from them, and move the result into the required subgroup. The stages are specified so implementations can produce compatible results.

sections.title: Uniform and Nonuniform Encodings
sections.content:
encode_to_curve hashes to one field element, maps it to a point, and clears the cofactor. Its output is nonuniform: some subgroup points cannot occur, and others have different probabilities.

hash_to_curve hashes to two field elements, maps each to a point, adds the points, and clears the cofactor. Its output is statistically close to uniform in the subgroup. Protocols that require a uniform random-oracle output must use this encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The faster encoding produces points with an uneven distribution. The uniform encoding does more work so its outputs are close to evenly distributed across the subgroup.

sections.title: Mappings and Recommended Suites
sections.content:
The RFC describes mappings for Weierstrass, Montgomery, and twisted Edwards curves. For Weierstrass curves it specifies Shallue-van de Woestijne and simplified SWU methods, including a variant for curves with A or B equal to zero. For Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves it recommends Elligator 2, with a rational map for the twisted Edwards form.

Recommended suites specify the curve, encoding type, field parameters, expansion function, mapping, and cofactor-clearing method. The RFC gives suites for NIST P-256, P-384, P-521, curve25519, edwards25519, curve448, edwards448, secp256k1, and BLS12-381.
sections.plainLanguage: Different curve equations need different mapping methods. A suite puts the required choices together so implementers can use a specified combination for a named curve.

sections.title: Domain Separation and Constant-Time Work
sections.content:
Every encoding must use a nonempty domain separation tag (DST). The tag separates one application's use from other uses; the RFC recommends a length of at least 16 bytes and including an application identifier and version.

Implementations should use constant-time operations so execution time and memory access do not depend on secret inputs. This is required when the input is secret and timing attacks are in scope. The RFC also warns that nonuniform encodings need security analysis and recommends uniform encoding when the needed distribution is unclear.
sections.plainLanguage: Each use needs its own label so it does not collide with another protocol's use. Constant-time operations help prevent an observer from learning about secret inputs by measuring execution.
